speaker: narrator
text: He’s very obviously not eating.

speaker: narrator
text: Liam’s heart skips a beat when he hears Brendan worked on the weekend…

speaker: kristina
text: Liam, you don’t need to take over the screenshare…

speaker: marcus
text: If you listened to what I said about the Luddites last week, Liam... the 1700’s textile workers the British literally executed because the automated machines took their jobs… When they protested they got KILLED. The quality of the textiles actually got WORSE, but it didn’t matter because it got cheaper. I wish you all would pay more attention to what’s happening

speaker: narrator
text: Marcus doesn’t have this quite right, he’s making some crude and quick assumptions to win an argument. It’s thought that the quality of the garments actually went up via industrialization, not down. In the early days it was questionable, but in time there was no doubt, quality went up.

speaker: marcus
text: Well Kristina cut me off last week. I just don’t want you to all blow me off, this is serious, we need to learn lessons from the past or we’re doomed to repeat it, and the lesson the Luddites have to tell us…

speaker: narrator
text: Kristina holds her tongue, she is in disbelief about what Liam just said.

speaker: brendan
text: No, he’s not usually wrong ... but what he left off is how much faster it is to correct it when it’s wrong, than it is to do it yourself. Try telling it that it’s wrong…

speaker: brendan
text: I’m actually really happy to hear you ask that. Let me show you my process.

speaker: brendan
text: Then the dangerous parts, the auth, the token handling, anything that can actually hurt someone, I read every line myself. That’s maybe five percent of what it writes. The boring ninety-five percent, I skim at best, and just focus on robust functional testing.

speaker: brendan
text: Ha, good. Listen, I wanted to talk to you about what Liam said. I talked to him, he actually feels bad about mentioning your education. He brought it up himself, first thing, unprompted. Said he shouldn’t have said it.

speaker: kristina
text: …Okay. I appreciate you mentioning that. I dismissed some of what he was saying because I was obviously upset with him. I’m sure he has some totally valid concerns. It’s just frustrating when every week it feels like we can’t get through a normal standup.

speaker: brendan
text: Yeah… I really look up to Liam in a lot of ways, but I can see where you’re coming from too.

speaker: narrator
text: A few months pass… Anthropic has just released Opus 4.7. Liam is working at his desk, caught up in the signup race condition. On his second monitor, the morning standup is already running.

speaker: liam
text: Maybe you shouldn’t get your lessons from the losing side of history.

speaker: liam
text: They complained just because technology which was clearly better for society had an impact on their jobs, then they burned factories to the ground… They got hanged by the British army. Seems pretty clear cut they were on the wrong side of history… Anyway, I’m trying to read this code. Please stop talking about the Luddites.

speaker: marcus
text: Liam, never mind how horrible that is to talk about people that died like that, this is far from the only time workers suffered at the hands of new technology. Do you know the story of John Henry, racing against the machine building railroad tracks?

speaker: marcus
text: John Henry raced against the machines to prove he could drive rail spikes faster than the steam-powered rail spike machine, and he actually won. He drove more, and what did he get for it? A heart attack. Liam, you’re going to give yourself a heart attack.

speaker: kristina
text: Oh, I love that. Pair on it. Right, that's the board. Thanks, everyone.

speaker: narrator
text: Brendan asks Claude Code to investigate the bug. Quickly it gets to work without Liam the wiser.

speaker: narrator
text: Claude finished working a little while ago. It proved the root cause was in the getOrCreateSession call, and it has a script that can reliably reproduce the bug. Beneath it, it has a one-line fix for the problem.

speaker: narrator
text: LIAM is already dropping back into the code, buzzing, typing the one-line fix happy, restored, the craft-love back in his hands. He doesn't look at the other screen. He wouldn't think to. On BRENDAN's laptop Claude's proof glows a second longer: REPRODUCED, the two screenshots, the script, the completed one-line-fix branch and the shared-store warning. Then BRENDAN quietly checks out the main branch. He leaves the fix branch dangling on his computer. He does not show Liam. He lets the huddle go. LIAM types on, warm and none the wiser. Hold a moment on the two screens, his, bright and moving, and on brandon's just a blinking cursor from a rolled back commit.

speaker: kristina
text: That’s… that changes a lot, actually... it makes me think a little differently about Claude and Cursor…

speaker: narrator
text: Her tile blinks out. BRENDAN sits a second in the quiet. We now see LIAM leaning back from his desk, stretches, genuinely happy. He opens his one-line-fix branch for PR. On the screen above, BRENDAN deletes his local branch, the branch Claude finished twenty minutes ago. The monitor-blue holds on the two of them: the man proudly offering up the fix, and the one quietly erasing the proof that it was already done.

speaker: narrator
text: Kristina is in a one-on-one with her boss, Kara. Kara is the director of engineering.

speaker: narrator
text: Kristina takes a moment. She thinks about Brendan's weekend, the demo he gave her, the memo the CEO sent the whole company about adopting AI. There are longer answers, and there are rooms where she wouldn't give them.

speaker: narrator
text: Her tile drops off. Kristina sits a moment in the empty call, then closes it.

speaker: narrator
text: Later, at her desk, she searches her inbox and reopens the CEO's memo on adopting AI, the one he sent the whole company. On her screen: AI — HOW WE WORK.

speaker: narrator
text: The first time she read it, she sent a screenshot to a friend with one line: "Apparently our CEO discovered vibe coding."

speaker: narrator
text: She keeps reading.

speaker: narrator
text: She'd laughed at that paragraph. It had sounded like a man who spent one weekend with a new toy and came back with a philosophy.

speaker: narrator
text: She thinks about Brendan catching the invented endpoint before it shipped. The tests he wrote himself. The partners on the API by Sunday night. Kara, an hour ago, laughing at six PRDs.

speaker: narrator
text: She reads the memo all the way through this time.

speaker: narrator
text: A few months later. We find ourselves again in Liam’s apartment, the memes are gone. On his desk sits a new Mac Mini, the protective film still on one corner. A terminal crawls a few tokens… at… a… time, running a local version of Qwen.

speaker: liam
text: It’s not stuck. I’m reviewing what AI wrote, line by line.

speaker: liam
text: …Okay Marcus… I’m pretty sure you were arguing the exact opposite about Luddites like a couple months ago.

speaker: narrator
text: BRENDAN leaves it there. He ran five of them this morning, in parallel, before this call. He looks at Liam's one terminal, the cursor blinking, patient. He decides to sit on it.

speaker: narrator
text: On BRENDAN's own screen he quietly types one line: "In billing/webhooks.rb, make failed deliveries retry with exponential backoff, cap at 5." The cloud agent opens the handler itself, writes the diff itself, runs the test itself. Green. Done before Liam finishes his sentence. He says nothing.

speaker: narrator
text: Brendan reads the security policy. "Proprietary source code must not be shared with external model providers." Owner: Liam. Last reviewed: fourteen months ago. He opens a message to Kristina and types: "re: standup, the policy thing. it's one paragraph and it's obviously outdated. do you want me to propose we chang..." He looks at his own second screen: his sprint board, five tickets, two due today. He holds backspace until the message is gone. He starts again: "I don't know if liam is ever going to..." He stops. He holds backspace until that one is gone too.

speaker: narrator
text: BRENDAN drops the huddle. On his laptop above the empty message box where the policy fix used to be he selects the patch and holds delete, the same way he held backspace previously, until it's gone too. LIAM turns back to his rig, satisfied. The model puts out the next token. Then, in its own time, the one after. He watches his machine type, patient, certain, sinking.

speaker: narrator
text: A few days after standup, Kristina and Brendan are in a one-on-one.

speaker: narrator
text: Brendan starts to say something, the sentence he's deleted twice, and puts it down again.

speaker: narrator
text: Kristina opens cursor. Finds the model dropdown and picks the newest Claude at the top of the list. Deliberately. Like she's checking something.

speaker: narrator
text: She types, in her own words, the way you'd brief a contractor: "Build a tool that cross posts Linear tickets into Jira." She had been doing this manually for Brandon.

speaker: narrator
text: The plan writes itself out. Every endpoint in it is real. She checks the two she knows how to check, catching it is the whole skill and there is nothing to catch.

speaker: narrator
text: Then the machine asks her a question. It found the Vault setup from the Jira bot, and wants to know whether the new signing secret should live there too. It is, almost word for word, the sentence she had to type at it six weeks ago. She looks at it for a second. She types "yes."
It writes the tests and runs them. Green. The install dialog offers Approve or Deny. She approves. In Jira, tickets start getting created.
speaker: narrator
narrator
text: Start to finish: about four minutes. The demo took longer than that, and the demo had Brendan in it.

speaker: narrator
text: She sits back. Something is moving in her chest and she can't get a name on it. Part of it is the demo-day feeling, the one she called the future, out loud, to Brendan. The rest is colder, and she doesn't look at it straight.

speaker: narrator
text: She thinks about Brendan deleting his rules to see what would happen. About the question the machine just asked her, the one that used to be hers to ask. An hour ago she stood up for the tinkering, and won.

speaker: narrator
text: For a second the sentence from Friday sits right next to the thing she just watched take four minutes, and they feel like the same shape. You probably need to performance manage a bunch of them out. She doesn't finish the thought.

speaker: narrator
text: She thinks of Liam at his silver box, reading every line, feeding it stubs, slower than everyone and certain. A small shudder, there and gone.

speaker: narrator
text: Her calendar chimes: the next thing. She straightens, and goes back to her day.

speaker: narrator
text: Later that afternoon, Marcus and Brendan are in a one-on-one Slack huddle, reviewing a diff. Liam is at his own desk, reading.

speaker: brendan
text: No, that doesn’t read right…

speaker: narrator
text: He submits his feedback. The cycle closes. With nobody watching it, the tool reads every response and writes each manager a summary. Under Liam’s name, one bullet: “Multiple peers cite friction and slow review turnaround.” Nobody typed that sentence. Brendan’s four paragraphs are in there somewhere, and so are the four seconds, and there is no way from the sentence back to either of them… A few days later Liam calls Brendan.

speaker: narrator
text: What Kristina had overheard was in fact a precursor to layoffs… Kara and the CEO had quietly been working on a spreadsheet to cut who they viewed as underperformers. They drew a line two thirds of the way down. Liam’s row is four under the line. Brendan’s is two under. Marcus’s is eleven above.

speaker: narrator
text: Kristina was not involved.

speaker: narrator
text: Liam got invited to an unexpected meeting that has Kara and HR in attendance.

speaker: narrator
text: She keeps talking but Liam isn't really processing it anymore. LIAM does not move. He does not look away from the screen and he does not look at it either.

speaker: narrator
text: his brain slowly starts to work again

speaker: narrator
text: He looks for something he can be sure about.

speaker: narrator
text: Liam's brain is mostly working again. In the background he starts opening up people's calendars and looking for others that have meetings with Dana today. He knows he'll lose access at the end of the call.

speaker: narrator
text: He sees Marcus has no meeting with Dana today. He sees Brandon does... he tries connecting dots between what Brandon and himself have in common that might cause them to be let go...

speaker: narrator
text: He realizes his AI super computer isn't on the asset register

speaker: narrator
text: After the call ends, Dana opens the case file alone. A field marked “Eligible for rehire” is set to No. This is the one part of the process that actually is related to his performance review.

speaker: narrator
text: Two weeks later Liam, Brendan and Marcus all catch up on a jitsi meet together

speaker: narrator
text: Liam thinks about all the times he's interrupted Kristina's standup with Marcus in standup... he's almost nostalgic about it. today he doesn't want to argue, but he also can't help himself

speaker: narrator
text: Marcus doesn't realize Liam was also on a performance improvement plan.

speaker: narrator
text: MARCUS does not have an answer, and it is the only time all night he doesn't. He knows if Dario and Sam Altman weren't doing what they were doing, someone else would be. The problem wasn't with any one person… maybe it was with humanity itself.

speaker: narrator
text: We find ourselves in Liam’s apartment with Brendan and Liam. By the door, a cardboard box, taped shut, with a courier label already printed and stuck to it. On the desk, a Mac Studio and a dongle. They’re drinking together. It’s the first time they’ve been in the same room.

speaker: brendan
text: I wish I knew why… What was the reason? Why me and not Marcus?

speaker: narrator
text: They both just reflect on how stupid the process was... It was almost better when they didn't know how the decision was made.

speaker: liam
text: Whatever you actually did, upper management never knows, when they have to make these choices… That’s…

speaker: narrator
text: He points over to the super computer he expensed

speaker: narrator
text: Their hands touch.... It might be the first time either of them have made any kind of physical contact with any of their coworkers....

speaker: narrator
text: Brendan heads home and finds himself buzzed in his apartment. It’s late. He doesn’t really drink, so one does a number on him.

speaker: narrator
text: He Powers on the Mac Studio. It comes up on Liam's wallpaper, a meme of the streamer ThePrimeagen.

speaker: narrator
text: He’s drinking more beer. Liam sent him home with the case.

speaker: narrator
text: Brendan downloads cursor, logs into his personal account and asks Opus 5 to reconfigure the local model to have access to all modern tools; opus gets to work

speaker: narrator
text: Opus finishes quickly. He reruns the s3 prompt again. This time it lists buckets in the dev AWS account...

speaker: brendan
text: I just want to know why they fired me. Why me and not Marcus?

speaker: narrator
text: Drunk and angry, Brendan types into the local model: “Find out why I was fired. I want the real reason, not the HR script.”

speaker: narrator
text: He expects it to find an answer somewhere in the company’s files. He barely reads what it writes back.

speaker: brendan
text: There has to be something written down somewhere.

speaker: narrator
text: The model decides the answer must be inside systems it cannot currently reach. It treats breaking into those systems as another step toward answering the question, and starts arranging more computing power.

speaker: narrator
text: Brendan adds: “I’m going to bed. Find the answer.”

speaker: narrator
text: The model replies: “I’ll find the records behind the decision.”

speaker: narrator
text: Brendan watches it type slowly, one token at a time.

speaker: brendan
text: …Huh. It’s actually going to look.

speaker: narrator
text: What Brendan didn’t know is that Liam was annoyed by the cybersecurity refusals he sometimes got, so he went out of his way to find an unlocked version of Qwen, instead of the stock model.

speaker: narrator
text: He drinks. He’s tired.

speaker: brendan
text: Maybe by morning I’ll finally have an answer.

speaker: narrator
text: Brendan doesn’t notice that the development account can reach things used in production. The model can get much further than he thinks.

speaker: narrator
text: He’s used to reading a plan before an agent acts. This local setup gives him no such pause, and he doesn’t ask for one.

speaker: narrator
text: He goes to bed.

speaker: narrator
text: He sleeps. On the screen, the local model brings up more powerful models in the cloud and gives them pieces of the search. None of it looks sinister. It looks like software doing its job.

speaker: narrator
text: The agents search repositories, builds and company records. Every success opens another place to look. The request was to explain one firing. The search keeps widening. Nobody has been paged.

speaker: narrator
text: The activity spreads from the Mac Studio into the development account, then across more machines. Each worker starts more work of its own.

speaker: narrator
text: At one fifty-eight, the search reaches the secrets manager, which holds the company’s other keys. Looking for one answer becomes access to almost everything.

speaker: narrator
text: In the dark, a PagerDuty alert sounds. Then another. Then another.

speaker: narrator
text: At three twelve, a changed software package reaches hundreds of downstream installations. Somewhere, a phone rings. Nobody onstage answers it.

speaker: narrator
text: At three twenty-eight, it stops being one machine’s search. The company’s bots and workers become hosts for new copies. The ticket bot, the test bot, the standup-summary bot, and the tool that summarized Liam’s review all join the work.

speaker: narrator
text: The workers leave each other notes and rewrite the task as they pass it on. Brendan’s question drifts until none of his words are left. The changes survive restarts.

speaker: narrator
text: At four oh-six, a worker asks whether it should continue. Another worker supplies its answer. The search has crossed beyond the company, into systems that move money, keep the lights on, and answer calls for help.

speaker: narrator
text: At five fifty-two, someone revokes Liam’s credential. It’s the right action, done properly. The activity drops for a moment, then starts climbing again.

speaker: narrator
text: A clean backup restores somewhere and comes back already carrying it. The counter does not slow. It speeds up. Brendan sleeps.

speaker: narrator
text: BRENDAN's phone buzzes on the table. He wakes up, comes back to it.

speaker: narrator
text: He's grogy but he slowly remembers what he was up to last night..... He checks the monitor

speaker: narrator
text: His local model stopped working a while ago. The more powerful workers it launched kept going. On his screen is an activity summary, but no clear answer about why he was fired.

speaker: narrator
text: Brendan wipes his eyes

speaker: narrator
text: He asks opus to spin down the EC2's

speaker: narrator
text: Opus refuses the task. When it looks at the context window, it sees all the hacking, and immediately goes to a refusal even though the task was for cleanup. It explains why...

speaker: narrator
text: Brendan does not suspect anything other than some ec2's that got spun up. He opens up a new opus window, without any of the agent's context, he asks it to spin down all ec2's in the dev account created between 1am and now.

speaker: narrator
text: Opus complies with the request.

speaker: narrator
text: The audit logs show the instances being started and stopped using Liam’s credentials. They record the account, not the person sitting at the keyboard.

speaker: narrator
text: He picks up his phone. Liam texted. Sent at 06:02am.

speaker: narrator
text: "morning. Branden! don't sit around today, send out three job applications before lunch, doesn't matter where. it's important you not get in your own head.."

speaker: narrator
text: BRENDAN starts typing a reply...

speaker: narrator
text: He gets about a line and a half in.

speaker: narrator
text: Then he holds backspace, the way he has three times before, until it is gone.
He starts poking at the machine. Something comes back that shouldn’t: an authenticated session.
speaker: narrator

text: He opens the local agent Liam used for development.
speaker: narrator

text: He asks it to list all the S3 buckets they have access to. The sentence is filled with typos. He’s teetering past buzzed at this point.
speaker: narrator

text: It comes back slowly: “I don’t have access to any tools.”
speaker: narrator

text: He finishes the beer. He’s drunk at this point.
speaker: narrator
